sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two Sum asks for two different elements whose values add to a target, usually returning their indexes. A one-pass solution stores values already seen in a map.

At index `i`, compute `needed := target-nums[i]`. If `needed` is already in the map, return its earlier index and `i`; otherwise store the current value and index.

For example, for `[2, 7, 11, 15]` and target `9`, the scan stores `2` at index zero, then finds that `9-7` is already present and returns `[0,1]`.

The contract must say whether exactly one solution exists, what to return when none exists, and whether any valid pair or all pairs are required. The standard one-pass method returns one pair.

Use the one-pass map when the input is unsorted, expected linear time matters, and O(n) extra space is acceptable. It preserves original indexes without rearranging the slice.

sections.title: The core model: the Two Sum problem in Go
sections.content:
the Two Sum problem in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The map contains exactly the elements to the left of the current index. That invariant guarantees a found complement uses a different, earlier position. Because each item performs a constant expected number of map operations, the scan is expected linear time.

```mermaid
  A[Read current value] --> B[Compute target - value]
  B --> C{Complement in seen map?}
  C -- yes --> D[Return earlier and current indexes]
  C -- no --> E[Store current value and index]
  E --> A
```

sections.content:
The useful question is not whether the Two Sum problem in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

The map method is designed for unsorted data where indexes matter. Sorting plus two pointers can reduce auxiliary lookup storage in some settings, but sorting changes order and needs a way to recover original indexes. For one interview-sized slice, the map is normally the clearest match.

Failures around the Two Sum problem in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

The order of two lines controls correctness. If the current value enters the map first, a lookup can find the same element. With `[3,3]`, check-then-store succeeds on the second index; with a single `[3]`, it correctly finds nothing.
